newsitem.title: USA: U.N. Security Council maintains Iraq sanctions.
newsitem.headline: U.N. Security Council maintains Iraq sanctions.

text.p: The United Nations Security Council on Thursday maintained the tough economic sanctions imposed on Baghdad since its August 1990 invasion of Kuwait, diplomats said.
The decision was expected and followed a critical report three weeks ago by the U.N. Special Commission (UNSCOM), which oversees Iraqi disarmament.
Diplomats also said that the U.S. delivered a sharply critical speech at Thursday's Security Council session, making it clear that its position on Iraq was not softening.
The main condition for any lifting of the sanctions is a clean bill of health from UNSCOM.

In his latest report, which was discussed in the Security Council Thursday but which diplomats have had since mid-April, UNSCOM's chief, Rolf Ekeus, said the Baghdad government said that Saddam Hussein's government must take "a major political decision...to give up, once and for all, all capabilities and ambition to retain or acquire proscribed weapons."

A U.S. statement, read in the Council on Thursday, said: "The last two months have seen an ongoing and concerted Iraqi effort to provoke the Council, to insult the Sanctions Committee and to play games with the clear requirements of the requirements of Resolution 661 (covering disarmament and other Gulf War settlement terms).
"Baghdad has not yet taken a political decision to end its weapons programs and stop its deliberate concealment and evasion activities," the U.S. statement, read by Ambassador Edward Gnehm, said.
Specifically, the U.S. said that Iraq continues to possess VX nerve gas and delivery systems, a view also expressed in the latest UNSCOM report.
"Nobody in (the Security Council) thinks (Iraq) is there yet. Nobody thinks they will be there in our lifetimes," said a U.S. official after Thursday's review.
A British diplomat reiterated that Iraq has not made progress on other vital issues either, including Kuwaiti missing persons and stolen property.
Russia, which has taken a generally softer line on Iraqi sanctions, noted in the Council that it is important to note the progress that Baghdad has achieved in the last six years.
The U.N. on Thursday swore in Australia's Ambassador, Richard Butler, as the new head of UNSCOM, replacing Rolf Ekeus, who is to go to Washington as Sweden's ambassador to the U.S.
Western diplomats said it was important to note that the Council's resolve on Iraq remains as firm as ever under the new UNSCOM head.
